title: MVVM Series: LiveData; the Superhero of Android Data Handling!
author: Hossein Jamshidi
content:
Hey there, fellow Android developers! Today, we're going to talk about a data-handling superhero – LiveData! It saves your app from data disasters and keeps your UI components in sync.

Tired of multi-source data mess? With LiveData, you can have a single source of truth for all your app's data. Just encapsulate your data in a LiveData object and let it do the heavy lifting.

LiveData is lifecycle-aware, which means it updates your UI components only when they're in the active state. Say goodbye to unnecessary UI updates and memory leaks.

Here is a simple example of using LiveData in Kotlin:

// Creating a LiveData object with some initial data
val myLiveData = MutableLiveData<String>().apply {
    value = "Han Solo!"
}

Somewhere else in your app, you may update the LiveData by:

button.setOnClickListener {
    val anotherName = "Luke Skywalker"
    model.currentName.setValue(anotherName)
    // Or use model.currentName.postValue(anotherName)
}
Note from Google: Call setValue(T) from the main thread. If executing on a worker thread, use postValue(T) instead.

Observing the LiveData object in a Fragment/Activity:

myLiveData.observe(viewLifecycleOwner, { data ->
    // Update UI with the latest data
    textView.text = data
})

LiveData provides two types – MutableLiveData (writable) and LiveData (read-only). Use MutableLiveData in ViewModels and expose only LiveData to UI components for a unidirectional data flow.

Note: Store LiveData in ViewModel objects, not activities or fragments, to avoid bloated UI controllers and survive configuration changes.

Start observing in onCreate() of the Fragment/Activity to avoid redundant calls.

For more information: developer.android.com/topic/libraries/architecture/livedata

This article was part of the Android MVVM series.

title: Compile C/C++ for Android and Make a Native Executable
author: Hossein Jamshidi
content:
Most of us are familiar with Android Studio or the Android SDK to develop Android apps, but what about native binary executables? Let's say you have a C program and you want to compile and run it on your Android phone just like a console application.

#include <stdio.h>
int main()
{
    printf("Hello world \n");
    printf("I'm running on Android\n");
    return 0;
}

First, get the cross-compiler:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install build-essential
sudo apt-get install gcc-arm-linux-gnueabihf

We assume your Android phone has an ARM CPU. This installs an ARM C compiler that lets you compile on an x86 host and produce an ARM executable binary. You don't need a full IDE — a text editor like GEdit works fine.

Create a file named hello.c. Open a terminal in the same folder and run:

arm-linux-gnueabi-gcc -static -march=armv7-a hello.c -o hello

This produces a binary named hello. Transfer it to your phone via ADB push. Run it from ADB shell:

./hello

Or launch it from your own app:

Process process = Runtime.getRuntime().exec("/sdcard/yourfolder/[filename]");

You may need to grant execute permission first:

chmod +x hello
Security note: Avoid chmod 777 in production. It makes the file readable, writable, and executable by all users — a significant security risk. Use it only for local testing.

If you're interested in integrating C++ with your Java/Kotlin app, check out the Android NDK guides.
